content: Cluttering, also known as tachyphemia, is a speech and communication disorder characterized by speech that is challenging for listeners to comprehend. This difficulty arises due to a rapid speaking rate, erratic rhythm, poor syntax or grammar, and the inclusion of words or phrases unrelated to the sentence. Historically, cluttering has been classified as a fluency disorder. Individuals with cluttering often exhibit a short attention span, poor concentration, disorganized thinking, difficulty listening, and a lack of awareness that their speech is unintelligible. Cluttering is sometimes mistaken for stuttering, as both disrupt the normal flow of speech. However, while stuttering is primarily a speech disorder, cluttering is considered a language disorder. A person who stutters has coherent thoughts but struggles to articulate them, whereas a person who clutters can verbalize their thoughts but does so in a disorganized manner. Cluttering affects not only speech but also thought patterns, writing, typing, and conversational skills. Stutterers typically experience dysfluency at the beginning of speech and become more fluent as they progress through their utterances. In contrast, clutterers are most intelligible at the start of their speech but become less clear as their speaking rate increases and intelligibility decreases. Stuttering is often accompanied by physical struggle behaviors, such as excessive tension in the speech muscles, whereas cluttering is characterized by effortless speech production. For example, a stutterer attempting to say I want to go to the store might sound like I wa-wa-wa-want to g-g-go to the s-s-s-store, while a clutterer might produce slurred speech, drop or distort sounds (e.g., /r/ and /l/), and speak in a monotone voice that starts loudly but trails off into a murmur. Clutterers frequently have associated reading and writing difficulties, including sprawling, disorganized handwriting that poorly integrates ideas and spacing. One clutterer described the experience as chaotic, while another shared their struggles in an online support group. Cluttering is often confused with other conditions, such as language delay, language disorders, learning disabilities, and attention deficit disorders. While cluttering and stuttering may sound similar to the untrained ear, they are distinct disorders with different characteristics. Stutterers are typically highly aware of their disorder, perform worse under stress, struggle with short answers, and often have neat handwriting. Their therapy focuses on relaxation techniques and diverting attention away from speech. Stutterers are often introverted, were once fluent before developing stuttering, and have organized speech and good listening skills. In contrast, clutterers are usually unaware of their disorder, perform better under stress, struggle with long answers, and have hasty, repetitive, and messy handwriting. They exhibit little to no fear of their speech, are careless in their communication, and require therapy that emphasizes attention to speech details. Clutterers are often extroverted, were never highly fluent, and tend to speak disorganized, tangential, and grammatically incorrect sentences with frequent word substitutions. They are impatient listeners, frequently interrupt, and have poor conversational turn-taking skills. Treatment for cluttering is often more prolonged than for stuttering due to the clutterer's lack of awareness of their condition, which can lead to indifference or hostility toward speech-language pathologists. Delayed auditory feedback (DAF) is commonly used to encourage a more deliberate and exaggerated oral-motor response. Other therapeutic approaches include improving narrative structure through storytelling exercises, practicing conversational turn-taking, pausing techniques, and language therapy. Historically, cluttering has been documented as early as the legend of Battaros, a Libyan king who spoke quickly and disorganizedly. The term battarismus was used to describe similar speech patterns. In the 1960s, cluttering was referred to as tachyphemia, derived from the Greek term for fast speech, though this term is no longer used as rapid speech is not a required feature of cluttering. Deso Weiss described cluttering as the outward manifestation of a central language imbalance and used the term Central Language Imbalance (CLI) synonymously with cluttering. Over the past two decades, researchers such as Kenneth O. St. Louis, Lawrence J. Raphael, Florence L. Myers, and Klaas Bakker have worked to standardize the definition of cluttering. Judith Kuster has compiled extensive resources on cluttering in her Stuttering Homepage. The first conference dedicated to cluttering, The First World Conference on Cluttering, was held in May 2007 in Razlog, Bulgaria, with over 60 participants from North America, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia. The conference also awarded the first Deso Weiss Award for Excellence in Cluttering to Kenneth St. Louis for his contributions to the understanding of the disorder. Cluttering is often associated with phenomena such as spoonerisms, malapropisms, Colemanballs, and Freudian slips. The term stuttering is sometimes used colloquially to refer to cluttering, especially when the speaker is nervous, as nervous speech often resembles cluttering more than stuttering. Individuals with ADD or ADHD may exhibit symptoms similar to cluttering, such as inattention, restlessness, impatience, and a short temper. Deso Weiss suggested that historical figures such as Battaros, Demosthenes, Pericles, Justinian, Bismarck, and Winston Churchill were clutterers. He noted that these individuals viewed the world holistically and were not overly preoccupied with minor details.
